claims.claim: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units, but carefully.
People living in subdivided flats have very little choice.
The numbers show that subdivided unit tenants are still being squeezed.
About 110,000 households live in subdivided units.
Subdivided units are small cubicles, often with shared kitchens and bathrooms.
The median rent of subdivided units is about 30 percent lower than a normal private flat.
Tenants of subdivided units pay 15 to 25 percent more per square foot.
Subdivided unit tenants are mostly new arrivals, single-parent households, and people waiting for public housing.
The average wait for public housing is around five and a half years.
For these tenants, a subdivided unit is not a real choice but what they have while waiting in the queue.
People with no alternatives cannot bargain with a landlord, which is the usual reason to have rent rules.
The current rules have not stopped rents from rising quickly.
Rent per square foot in subdivided units went up 6.8 percent in 2019 to 2021 and another 3.1 percent in 2021 to 2023.
General private rent grew only 2.4 and 1.7 percent in the same periods.
The 2021 ordinance seems to have slowed the rise, but subdivided rents still grew faster than the rest of the market.
The share of income spent on rent for these households got worse, going from 31 to 34 percent.
The usual argument against stricter control is that landlords will leave the market and the supply of units will shrink.
The data does not show that landlords have left the market so far.
The estimated stock of subdivided units went from 100,800 units in 2019 to 111,200 in 2025.
The stock kept growing through the 2021 ordinance.
The data does not prove the rules were harmless.
The stock could have grown for other reasons, such as high demand from people stuck in the queue.
A tighter rule than the 2021 one might act differently from a moderate one.
The numbers give no sign yet that moderate control caused landlords to leave.
The sensible step is a measured tightening, for example a limit on how much rent can rise between tenancies, and not a hard cap that is very strict.
Tenants have few options, pay a premium for their space, and their rent burden is getting heavier.
The supply risk is real but not visible in the evidence.
A moderate change lets the government check the stock figures each year and step back if units start to disappear.
Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units in a moderate way.
The tenants are stuck and paying more than they should.
Their burden is rising faster than the wider market.
The stock has kept growing under the current rules.
